## 6.3 United States — 2,115 reviews (29.92%), mean 3.65★ — eligible

Just under a third of the corpus, and the storefront where the Google glue is strongest and the family gap widest.

| Theme | US | Global | Read |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `PR_GOOGLEINT` | 9.41% | 7.24% | **1.3×** — Gmail/Calendar integration is a US story |
| `U_HABIT_USE` | 10.73% | 8.43% | daily-routine use above average |
| `U_HABIT_TRACK_GAP` | 5.20% | 4.53% | slightly above global |
| `NEG_NO_SHARE` | 7.61% | 6.42% | family sharing is a US complaint |
| `SEG_WORK` | 5.53% | 3.92% | **1.4×** — the Workspace audience |
| `SW_NAMED` | 8.46% | 6.04% | **1.4×** — most competitor talk of any large market |
| `U_LEAVE_INTENT` | 3.97% | 2.73% | **1.5×** — the US leaves most readily |
| `NEG_NO_WIDGET` | 3.97% | 5.90% | below global |
| `NEG_LISTS` | 3.93% | 4.40% | below global |

**The US is where Tasks is used most seriously and compared most often.** It is the only large storefront where leave-intent exceeds 3%, and the competitor it is compared to is Microsoft To Do, Todoist and Apple Reminders in that order. A US-only read of this corpus would over-weight competitive churn and under-weight the list-management friction that dominates Japan and Russia.

## 6.4 Japan — 620 reviews (8.77%), mean 3.69★ — eligible

The second storefront by volume and the one where the *interface* — not the feature set — is the complaint.

| Theme | JP | Global | Read |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `NEG_LISTS` | 10.32% | 4.40% | **2.3× — the highest of any large storefront**: cannot reorder lists on iOS |
| `PR_SIMPLE` | 15.81% | 12.42% | simplicity is valued more here |
| `U_RELIABILITY` | 23.55% | 17.63% | **1.3×** — sync and crash complaints above global |
| `NEG_RECUR_BUG` | 5.00% | 3.25% | **1.5×** — the hidden-until-due repeat |
| `NEG_CROSSPLAT_BREAK` | 6.29% | 4.00% | 1.6× — the iOS app vs web gap |
| `NEG_NO_SHARE` | 2.90% | 6.42% | **0.45× — sharing barely matters in Japan** |
| `SEG_PARENT` | 0.32% | 1.09% | family coordination near-absent |
| `U_HABIT_USE` | 6.61% | 8.43% | below global |

**Japanese reviewers use Tasks as a personal list and want it to behave like one** — `13574791994` (#6525, 2025-12-30, jp, 1★) "「リストの並び替えがアプリではできない」と数えきれない人達が書いてるのに、なぜ改善しないのか" *["you can't reorder lists in the app" — countless people have written this, so why isn't it fixed?]*. The family/sharing complaint that drives the US and Europe is one-sixth as common. **Japan is also where the recurring-task behaviour is felt most as a routine failure**: `8506254691` (#3946, 2022-03-28, jp, 4★) "毎日のルーティーン管理に活用させて頂いています / 翌日欄に繰り越して表示できるようにしてもらえませんか" *[I use it to manage my daily routine / could you make it carry over and show in the next day's column?]*.

## 6.5 Where the habit-tracking gap is loudest

Eligible storefronts by `U_HABIT_TRACK_GAP` share (global 4.53%):

| Storefront | n | Gap share | vs global |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Russia** | **276** | **7.25%** | **1.6×** |
| **India** | **231** | **6.93%** | **1.5×** |
| Chile | 58 | 6.90% | 1.5× |
| Netherlands | 76 | 6.58% | 1.5× |
| Turkey | 77 | 6.49% | 1.4× |
| Philippines | 69 | 5.80% | 1.3× |
| **Brazil** | **311** | **5.79%** | **1.3×** |
| **Japan** | **620** | **5.32%** | **1.2×** |
| **United States** | **2,115** | **5.20%** | **1.1×** |
| Canada | 303 | 0.66% | 0.15× |
| Spain | 152 | 0.66% | 0.15× |
| Ukraine | 65 | 0.00% | — |

Only Russia, India, Brazil, Japan and the US among these carry enough reviews to be more than suggestive; Chile, the Netherlands, Turkey and the Philippines are eligible but small and their rates are directional.

**Russia is the sharpest case: the lowest praise rate of any eligible storefront (`U_PRAISE_ANY` 28.3%), the second-highest missing-capability rate (56.5%, after Germany's 57.7%), and a habit gap 1.6× global** — `9203967181` (#4352, 2022-10-20, ru, 4★) "приходится дублировать задачи в Напоминания" *[I have to duplicate tasks into Reminders]*; `8501131135` (#3943, 2022-03-27, ru, 3★) "Прошу добавить возможность создания целей / двигаться к своим целям и отслеживать прогресс по выполненным задачам" *[please add the ability to create goals / move toward my goals and track progress on completed tasks]*. **India** pairs the second-highest habit gap with the highest daily-routine use of any large market outside the US (`U_HABIT_USE` 10.4%): `14232461252` (#6917, 2026-06-27, in, 5★) "i never skip my task  due to this app"; `12100262658` (#5881, 2024-12-24, in, 4★) asks for completion timestamps and weekly statistics.

**Canada and Spain are the anomaly** — both eligible, both at 0.66% — and neither has an obvious explanation in the text; Canada's complaint is sharing (10.9%) and Calendar sync (10.2%), Spain's is `NEG_FEATURELESS` (13.2%, the highest of any eligible storefront).

## 6.6 Sharing is a Western-and-Latin complaint; list order is an East-Asian one

`NEG_NO_SHARE` across eligible storefronts (global 6.42%):

| High | | Low | |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| France | 13.29% | South Korea | 0.00% |
| Chile | 12.07% | Thailand | 0.00% |
| Spain | 11.84% | Vietnam | 0.00% |
| Colombia | 11.67% | Taiwan | 2.11% |
| Canada | 10.89% | Japan | 2.90% |
| Poland | 10.53% | Brazil | 3.22% |
| Israel | 10.45% | Russia | 3.62% |
| Germany | 9.14% | | |

`NEG_LISTS` (cannot reorder lists on iOS) runs the other way: Japan 10.32%, Russia 8.0%, Germany 6.9%, Korea 5.3%, against 2.3–2.7% in Canada, Brazil, the UK and India. And `NEG_NO_WIDGET` is highest in Indonesia (32.0%, n=50), Philippines (15.9%), Korea (12.4%) and Russia (12.3%).

**Two mechanisms are visible and should not be conflated.** The sharing demand comes from reviewers describing a partner or family (`SEG_PARENT` 2.0% in the US, 0.3% in Japan, 0.0% in Korea); the list-order demand comes from reviewers with many lists. Whether that reflects household structure, how the app is marketed, or simply who writes reviews in each market, the corpus cannot say, and no causal claim is made.

## 6.7 High-volume markets, and the corpus-versus-public gap

**Definition, disclosed:** no spend data was available, so the high-volume group is defined by **public rating count** from `Tools/native_ratings.json` — a volume proxy, explicitly **not** downloads and **not** revenue.

The ten highest-volume storefronts (US, JP, BR, CA, GB, IN, KR, AU, MX, FR) hold **4,425 corpus reviews (62.60%)**.

**The gap is the headline of this section.** Across the 104 storefronts in the corpus:

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Public ratings | **353,516** |
| Public weighted mean | **4.7627★** |
| Corpus text reviews | 7,069 |
| Corpus mean | **3.6905★** |
| **Gap** | **+1.0722★** |
| Text reviews as share of ratings | **2.000%** |

Every eligible storefront shows a positive gap. The widest are **the United Kingdom (+1.43★)**, **Poland (+1.43★)** and **Germany (+1.38★)** — the three storefronts where `NEG_FEATURELESS` and `U_MISSING_ANY` run highest; the narrowest are **Mexico (+0.64★)**, **South Korea (+0.68★)** and **Israel (+0.68★)**.

**Read every negative rate in this report as an upper bound.** A reader who takes `U_MISSING_ANY` = 43.74% as "44% of Google Tasks users find it insufficient" will be wrong; the correct reading is "44% of the 2% of raters who wrote text named a missing capability." The gap here (+1.07★) is larger than for Apple Reminders (+0.87★), which is consistent with a downloaded app attracting more deliberate — and more critical — text reviewers than a pre-installed one.

## 6.8 Storefront is not language

Script family, derived mechanically from title+body (§9.F), not from storefront:

| Script | n | % |
|---|---:|---:|
| Latin | 5,755 | 81.41% |
| Japanese (kana present) | 600 | 8.49% |
| Cyrillic | 294 | 4.16% |
| Chinese (Han, no kana) | 160 | 2.26% |
| Korean (Hangul) | 159 | 2.25% |
| Thai | 35 | 0.50% |
| Hebrew | 33 | 0.47% |
| Arabic | 27 | 0.38% |
| Greek | 4 | 0.06% |
| No letters (emoji/punctuation only) | 2 | 0.03% |

**18.56% of the corpus is non-Latin script.** Latin script spans English, Spanish, Portuguese, German, French, Italian, Dutch, Polish, Turkish, Vietnamese, Swedish, Danish, Czech, Hungarian, Indonesian and more, so "Latin" is not "English".

A per-review hand language tag was recorded while reading. It is treated as a reading aid only and is used for no quantified claim; the mechanical script table above is what every language statement rests on.

## 6.9 Storefronts below 50 reviews — limited evidence

77 storefronts, 957 reviews (13.54%), pooled mean **3.70★** — in line with the corpus mean. Largest are Sweden (48), Singapore (47), China mainland (47), Malaysia (44), Saudi Arabia (43), Norway (42), Switzerland (40), Hong Kong (38).

**China mainland deserves one sentence and no more:** 27 of its 47 reviews are `NEG_CHINA` ("cannot connect", "even with a VPN"), 35 of the 47 are from 2018–2019, and its mean is 2.70★. That is a connectivity story from the launch period, not a product story, and it is below threshold.

**No standalone claim is made about any of them.** Where one contains a notable individual observation it is cited as an individual review — for example `13710924178` (#6607, 2026-02-04, kg, 5★) from Kyrgyzstan (below threshold) on a streak counter, quoted in §3.3 as one person's statement and not as evidence about Kyrgyzstan.

# PART 7 — TIME-TREND ANALYSIS

## 7.1 Method, and the era that is a different product

Eras are cut at the breakpoints the data itself shows — the quarters in which a dominant complaint collapses because the capability shipped. **There is no version field**, so these are calendar windows, not release cohorts.

| Era | Window | n | % | Mean | Votes/review | Median body | Defined by |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| **E1** launch | 2018-04-25 → 2019-03-31 | 835 | 11.81% | **2.957★** | 0.516 | 123 | no time-of-day, no repeats, no notifications, no iPad |
| **E2** time & repeat | 2019-04-01 → 2020-09-30 | 1,755 | 24.83% | 3.729★ | 0.585 | 93 | tasks still not in the Calendar app; no widget |
| **E3** calendar & widget | 2020-10-01 → 2023-03-31 | 2,049 | 28.99% | 3.913★ | 0.262 | 97 | the stable product; list tabs added |
| **E4** migration | 2023-04-01 → 2025-03-31 | 1,421 | 20.10% | 3.676★ | 0.339 | 109 | Calendar Reminders forced into Tasks; crash waves |
| **E5** recent | 2025-04-01 → 2026-09-18 | 1,009 | 14.27% | 3.798★ | 0.187 | 79 | Keep reminders forced into Tasks; deadline; Gemini; 2026 redesign |

**E1 is a real cohort, not a collection artefact.** Unlike the Apple Reminders corpus, volume (175 reviews in launch month, 40–110/month after), vote rate and body length are continuous across the E1/E2 boundary; E1's 2.957★ is what a launch without repeats, times or notifications earned. **It is still not comparable to E2–E5 as a product**, and §9.D re-runs every headline without it. Pooled rates for the three capabilities shipped in 2019-03 (`NEG_NO_TIME` 2.36%, `NEG_NO_RECUR` 1.58%, `NEG_NO_NOTIF` 1.75%) are almost entirely E1 and are **not** current complaints.

**One code pair is unusable for trend.** `PR_CALVIEW` and `PR_GOOGLEINT` drifted into each other from 2024Q2 (§1.4). Their union is used below and is flat: 7.66% (E1), 9.00%, 13.52%, 11.47%, 9.42% (E5).

| Code | E2 | E3 | E4 | E5 | Movement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `NEG_NO_SEARCH` | 3.82% | 3.90% | 6.76% | 6.44% | **rising, 1.7×** |

## 7.3 Five requests that were shipped, and what that looks like in the data

**Time-of-day, repeats, notifications — 2019-03.** `NEG_NO_TIME` runs 18.0% → 21.5% → 18.6% → 11.9% across the four launch quarters, then **0.4%** in 2019Q2 and never above 1.9% again. `NEG_NO_RECUR` 12.2% → 7.4% → 11.3% → 9.3% → **1.1%**. `PR_IMPROVED` spikes to 8.6% in 2019Q1 with a cluster dated 2019-03-20 to 03-22: `3904526245` (#812, 2019-03-20, de, 4★) — "Da man jetzt endlich auch Uhrzeiten und wiederkehrende Aufgaben erstellen kann" *[now that you can finally create times and recurring tasks]*; `3905846946` (#814, 2019-03-21, br, 5★) — "Obrigada por colocarem a opção de horário, era o que faltava" *[thank you for adding the time option, it was what was missing]*; `3907932052` (#818, 2019-03-21, us, 5★) — "Now we have a compelling tool". The corpus mean rises from 2.957★ (E1) to 3.729★ (E2).

**Tasks in the Calendar app — 2020Q4.** `NEG_CALSYNC` holds at 13–18.5% for seven consecutive quarters (2019Q1–2020Q3), then **4.7%** in 2020Q4 and 3.8% in 2021Q1. `7298765894` (#3232, 2021-05-04, de, 3★) — "Now that the tasks finally appear in the calendar app it's pretty awesome". The corpus mean rises again, 3.729★ → 3.913★.

**A widget — 2021Q1.** `NEG_NO_WIDGET` peaks at 24.8% in January 2021 (iOS 14 home-screen widgets had arrived the previous September and every other app had one), then 2.2% in 2021Q2. `PR_WIDGET` appears for the first time on 2021-03-05. The residual complaint from 2024 onward is *quality* — too small, one account, not interactive, no lock screen: `12334136653` (#5989, 2025-02-20, id, 4★) — "the widget is bigger and we could actually check the tasks without opening the app, just like apple reminders".

**Lists as tabs — 2021Q3.** `PR_LISTS` = 0 before 2021-08-26; three Japanese reviewers notice the change within a month. It later becomes a *loss* when the 2026 redesign removes the hamburger list menu (§7.5).

**Deadline, Gemini, Keep reminders — 2025Q4 → 2026.** `PR_IMPROVED` 2.08% in E5 (against 1.06% in E4); 26 Gemini mentions, 19 in 2026, mean 4.15★; `13445849401` (#6465, 2025-11-27, in, 5★) — "The new deadline feature, is what i needed for a very longtime". `13439643320` (#6463, 2025-11-25, us, 5★) — "It really helps that now is combined with Google keep reminders" — is the *positive* reading of the migration that §7.4 records as a wave of one-star reviews. March 2026 — Gemini capture plus the deadline feature, before the redesign — is the **highest monthly mean in the corpus: 4.29★** (n=62).

**This is what a shipped painkiller looks like: the ask collapses inside one quarter, the corpus mean steps up, and the praise that replaces it is about the app being *usable*, not about the feature.** Caution: no version field exists; these are quarters in which reviewers report the change, not release dates.

## 7.4 What broke, and when

**The September 2019 edit lock.** In the month iOS 13 shipped, **51 of the 57 `NEG_EDIT_BROKEN` reviews** were written — 38.9% of that month's 131 reviews — all saying the same thing: `4814171191` (#1357, 2019-09-21, us, 1★) "I'm unable to edit my tasks after the iOS update"; `4838114068` (#1394, 2019-09-26, jp, 5★) "各項目が編集できなくなってしまいました" *[each item has become uneditable]*. `BUGREPORT_VER` hits 28.2% that month. It was fixed within days — `4852130149` (#1417, 2019-09-28, it, 5★) "Dopo l'aggiornamento di oggi si possono modificare di nuovo le note" *[after today's update notes can be edited again]* — and October's mean is 3.98★, the highest of the year. **The cleanest resolved regression in the corpus, and the only one with a "thank you" cluster (`PR_SUPPORT` 3.1% that month).**

**The April 2022 sort change.** `NEG_REDESIGN` 13.1% and `NEG_NO_SORT` 14.8% in one month (n=61, mean 3.64★ against 4.00★ the month before): `8527933263` (#3955, 2022-04-03, us, 1★) — "the UI changed from something that was useful to something different with 0 explanation / Why are tasks sorted by the order I create them instead of their due date?"; `8558713654` (#3982, 2022-04-12, us, 3★) — "Really sad to see the delightful illustrations that began a new list and rewarded you for completing one".

**The 2023 Reminders migration (§3.7).** `NEG_REMINDERS_MIGRATION` 10.0% (May) and 7.4% (June); `NEG_NOTIF_FAIL` 7.4% (June) and 8.1% (August); July 2023 is the **lowest monthly mean in the corpus since the launch era — 3.30★** (n=66).

**Crash waves at iOS releases.** `NEG_CRASH` 15.4% (2023-01), 12.0% (2024-01), 10.5% (2025-02), 9.8% (2025-05). Each resolves within two months; each costs a leave-intent spike (`U_LEAVE_INTENT` 6.1% in 2023Q4, 5.3% in 2025Q2).

**The Keep reminders migration (2025-11 → 2026-02).** `NEG_REMINDERS_MIGRATION` 4.8% / 3.7% / 2.7% / 2.7% and `NEG_FRAGMENT` 4.8–5.3% for four months; `NEG_NOTIF_FAIL` 6.3% in November. Smaller than 2023, and running *alongside* the Gemini praise in the same months — `PR_GOOGLEINT` 10.7–14.9% — so the monthly mean barely moves (3.76–3.92★).

**The 2026 redesign.** `NEG_REDESIGN` 6.2% (May), 8.9% (August), 10.3% (September); `NEG_LISTS` 12.5% (August). The hamburger list menu and the centred "add" button went: `14561702660` (#7065, 2026-09-17, us, 1★) — "I absolutely despise that the little hamburger menu was taken away to flip through the many lists I have / I need to find a new now because this is no longer efficient"; `14566186839` (#7069, 2026-09-18, us, 2★) — "Left-handed people like myself prefer the "add task" button in the middle where it was accessible". `NEG_ACCESS` appears for the first time in months (3.6%, 3.4%). This is the corpus's most recent event and its full size cannot yet be known.

## 7.5 What got worse

**Search and list management are the two complaints that grow as the user base ages.** `NEG_NO_SEARCH` 3.82% (E2) → 6.44% (E5) and `NEG_LISTS` 2.85% → 5.35%, while `TENURE_LONG` rises 0.23% → 1.78%. Long-tenure users have long lists; long lists need search and order. `11681008550` (#5672, 2024-09-02, br, 2★) — "Sou usuário fiel há anos, mas o app tá parado no tempo / A versão web evoluiu, mas o app continua igual / Cadê a busca" *[I've been a loyal user for years, but the app is stuck in time / the web version evolved, but the app stays the same / where's search]*.

**"Abandoned" is said more each era.** `NEG_ABANDONED` 0.73% (E3) → 2.08% (E5): `12590859880` (#6113, 2025-04-27, kr, 3★) — "제발 ai에 쓰는 돈에 1/10000만 투자를" *[please invest just 1/10,000 of the money spent on AI]*; `14366663608` (#6979, 2026-07-30, us, 1★) — "It's in maintenance mode".

**Simplicity praise is thinning.** `PR_SIMPLE` 14.87% (E2) → 9.22% (E5) and `PR_DESIGN` 2.79% → 0.59%. The launch-era aesthetic ("Simple, fast, and beautiful" — `2466124565` #5, 2018-04-25, ch, 5★) is no longer remarked on; what remains is functional praise (`PR_ORGANISE`, `PR_LISTS`) and ecosystem praise.

**Notifications got less reliable, not more.** `NEG_NOTIF_FAIL` 1.94% (E2) → 3.17% (E4) → 2.78% (E5), with both migrations contributing.

## 7.6 What has not changed in seven years

- **`NEG_NO_SHARE` is flat at 4.8–7.8% across every era.** The single most-requested capability on launch day is the single most-requested capability today.
- **`REQ_VIEW` is flat at 3.8–5.4%.** A Today / all-lists view has been asked for in every quarter of the app's life.
- **`U_HABIT_TRACK_GAP` is flat at 3.0–5.2% per era**, and `NEG_RECUR_BUG` — the hidden-until-due repeat — at 2.9–5.1% since it became possible to set a repeat at all. The habit gap has not moved because the design decision behind it has not moved.
- **`NEG_BADGE` is flat at 1.6–2.5%.** No app-icon badge in 3,068 days.
- **`U_FREE_VALUE` is flat at 1.3–2.1%.** Free is neither growing nor eroding as a stated reason.
- **`MON_WOULD_PAY` never exceeds 10 reviews in any cut of the data.**

---

# PART 8 — PRODUCT IMPLICATIONS

Every recommendation names the findings behind it. Immediate fixes, experiments and research questions are kept separate. These are framed for **a team building a habit product against this incumbent**, which is the decision this analysis informs.

## 8.1 Do not compete on being a better list; compete on being the missing layer (§0.1, §0.2, §5.5)

`PR_SIMPLE` + `PR_ENOUGH` = 958 reviews (13.55%) describe an incumbent that is sufficient as a list. But `U_MISSING_ANY` = 3,092 (43.74%) says the *same* users find it insufficient as a system — and 133 of the 193 leave-intent reviews name a missing capability, not a failure.

**Implication:** the pitch is not "a better to-do list" (which loses to free and simple) and not "a more reliable one" (which is not the complaint). It is "the things Google Tasks will not do" — with Google Calendar sync as table stakes, because 986 reviewers (13.95%) say the Google glue is why they stay. A product that does not appear on Google Calendar starts 14% behind.

## 8.2 The wedge is the recurring task, and it is a design decision the incumbent has defended for seven years (§0.3, §0.4, §7.6)

`NEG_RECUR_BUG` = 230 (3.25%) and `HAB_FAIL` = 94 (4.7× leave lift) describe one mechanism: a repeating task vanishes on completion and reappears only on its next due date; it cannot carry subtasks; it cannot repeat relative to completion; it cannot end; it leaves no record. 84 of the 94 habit failures are this. The request has been made in every quarter since 2019Q2 and the behaviour is unchanged.

**Implication — build these five first, in this order:**
1. **Repeat-after-completion and arbitrary rules** (every N days from when I did it; Mon/Wed/Fri; last weekday; hourly within a window; with an end date). `REQ_FLEXFREQ` = 59 and the two reviewers who wrote Apps Script to get it (`7226394404` #3199, `14525362340` #7047).
2. **The next occurrence visible now.** "Hard to prepare the night before" (`9100572042` #4272). This is the single sentence that separates a task list from a routine tool.
3. **A persistent record of completion** — timestamp, a completed-on-calendar view, a count. `HAB_NOHIST` = 92, `REQ_PROGRESS` = 55; `13635879857` (#6569, 2026-01-15, pl, 3★) "the most rewarding thing (that basically all other apps have except for this one) is that I can see what I was able to do that day".
4. **A daily checklist that resets, and "uncheck all".** `REQ_RESET` = 19 + `NEG_NO_BULK` = 22; the packing-list and morning-routine use cases.
5. **A completion sound with an off switch.** `REQ_REWARD` = 26; and the 2026 lesson that removing one produced a one-star ADHD review (`14042352159` #6820).

Streaks are **not** on this list: `REQ_STREAK` = 3. Build the record; let the streak be a view of it.

## 8.3 Sharing is the family painkiller, and it is priced (§0.4, §3.4, §5.3)

`NEG_NO_SHARE` = 454 (6.42%), flat for seven years; 61 of 77 parents name it; it is the request most often tied to a named destination; and it is one of the two capabilities a reviewer offered to pay Google for. Third-party clients already charge for it on top of Google's own data (`7873505414` #3545).

**Implication:** a shared list — partner, household, small team — is a feature people leave a free app for and pay a third party to get. It belongs in the paid tier, and it should sync to Google Calendar for both parties.

## 8.4 Be the best iOS client of Google data, because Google is not (§3.11, §6.4, §7.5)

`NEG_CROSSPLAT_BREAK` = 283 (4.00%): the iPhone app cannot search, sort, reorder lists, or show subtasks the way the web can. `NEG_NO_SEARCH` is rising (6.44% in E5); `NEG_LISTS` is 10.32% in Japan. `NEG_ABANDONED` is rising.

**Implication:** parity-plus on iOS — search, sort, list order, badge, a usable widget, an Apple Watch app (`NEG_NO_WATCH` = 128) — is a differentiator against this incumbent specifically, and the users who want it say so in the second-largest storefront.

## 8.5 Never migrate users by force, and never remove a small delight (§3.7, §7.4)

Both forced migrations (2023 Reminders → Tasks; 2025 Keep → Tasks) produced multi-month waves of one-star reviews from people who had not chosen Tasks and now had to. The 2022 and 2026 redesigns each removed something small — a sort order, a completion sound, a list menu — and each produced a `NEG_REDESIGN` spike with a 3.9× leave lift.

**Implication:** import from Keep, Reminders, Tasks and paper on the user's initiative, never on the product's. Ship every removal behind a setting for at least one release.

## 8.6 Target the markets where the gap is loudest, not the biggest market (§6.3, §6.5, §6.6)

The US is 29.92% of the corpus and has the highest leave-intent (3.97%) and competitor-naming (8.46%) — a crowded, switching-prone market. Russia (7.25%), India (6.93%) and Brazil (5.79%) have the loudest habit gap; Japan has the loudest list-friction complaint; France, Spain and Latin America have the loudest sharing complaint.

**Implication:** US-only research will find a competitive-churn story. The habit story is in Russia, India and Brazil; the sharing story is in France, Spain, Chile and Colombia; the iOS-client story is in Japan.

## 8.7 Pricing: free core, one paid capability, low and optional (§0.6, §5.3, §5.4)

`MON_WOULD_PAY` = 10; the only price offered to Google is $1–2 AUD/month, "optional"; `MON_REFUSE_PAY` = 16; the incumbent is free and reviewers benchmark against it explicitly. The one thing people demonstrably pay for is a third-party layer that adds sharing, sorting, search or a desktop window to free Google data — at ~$15 one-time, $6/year, ¥1,500.

**Implication:** the list, the calendar sync and the routine mechanics of §8.2 must be free, or the product is compared to Google Tasks and loses. Charge for the capabilities the corpus shows people already paying third parties for — sharing (§8.3), cross-device polish (§8.4), history and progress views — and charge little. **Treat subscription resistance as the default; test a one-time price.** This is a hypothesis from 29 `MON_PAID_3P` reviews and 10 `MON_WOULD_PAY` reviews, not a finding, and needs pricing research.

## 8.8 Research questions this corpus raises but cannot answer

1. **Does the habit gap convert?** 320 reviewers want habit capabilities inside a free app; the habit-app vocabulary appears 30 times; a habit app is named once. Whether these users would recognise, install or pay for a product marketed as a habit tracker is unknown and must be measured directly.
2. **Why is medication absent?** `HAB_MED` = 11 (0.16%) against 1.44% for Apple Reminders. Is it notification unreliability, the date-only origin, or a different user base? The corpus cannot separate them.
3. **What is the real reliability rate?** Everything here is bounded by the +1.07★ non-response gap.
4. **Would the 193 leave-intent reviewers actually have left, and to where?** Review text captures intent at a moment of frustration; Microsoft To Do and Apple Reminders are named, but arrival is not observed.
5. **Are Canada and Spain (0.66% habit gap) real outliers or noise?** Both are eligible; neither has a visible explanation.

## 8.9 What to copy, and what not to

**Copy:** task-from-email and task-from-assistant capture (`PR_CAPTURE` 4.69★, Gemini mentions 4.15★); tasks on the calendar as a first-class view; instant cross-device sync (`PR_SYNC` 4.64★); the satisfaction of the check-off (`PR_PROGRESS` 4.90★); tabs for lists; a completed section that can be reviewed (`PR_COMPLETED` 4.85★); "not overly complicated" as a design constraint (`PR_SIMPLE` 12.42%).

**Do not copy:** a repeat that hides until due (§8.2); subtasks that cannot repeat, collapse or survive completion (`NEG_NO_SUBTASK` 293); a mobile client that trails the web (`NEG_CROSSPLAT_BREAK` 283); no badge (`NEG_BADGE` 143, seven years); "clear completed" that deletes a list with no undo (`NEG_DATALOSS` 51, 5.0× leave lift); forced migrations (§8.5); removing the completion sound (§8.2).

# PART 9 — EVIDENCE APPENDIX

## 9.A Counting rules

1. **Denominator.** Unless a sentence names a narrower scope, every percentage uses **7,069** — all reviews, all 104 storefronts, 2018-04-25 → 2026-09-18.
2. **Non-exclusive themes.** A review may carry any number of codes; mean is 2.61, maximum 18. Code percentages therefore sum to far more than 100%.
3. **Unions count once.** A review carrying `PR_FREE` and `MON_FREE_VALUE` counts once in `U_FREE_VALUE`.
4. **Segment rates are labelled.** "52.14% of one- and two-star reviews" uses 1,473 as denominator and says so. Segment rates never replace the global signal band.
5. **Mean rating of a code** is the mean star rating of the reviews carrying it. It describes who says a thing, not how good the thing is.
6. **`PR_GENERIC` and `NOISE` carry no interpretive weight.** `PR_GENERIC` (13.03%) is approval with no stated reason; `NOISE` (1.32%) is off-topic, test or content-free text. Both exist so that the specific codes stay clean.
7. **A `NEG_NO_*` code means "names this capability as absent or inadequate"**, whether phrased as a complaint or a request. There is no separate `REQ_` mirror for those capabilities, so a wish and a gripe about the same gap count once. `U_REQ_ANY` contains only the seven `REQ_` codes that have no `NEG_NO_*` counterpart plus the habit requests.
8. **`HAB_*` codes record behaviour, not intent.** `HAB_DAILY` means the reviewer says they run a daily list. It does **not** mean they are building a habit. This is the imposed-lens caveat of §1.6.6, and it is why §0.3 rests on `U_HABIT_TRACK_GAP` (a stated missing capability) and `HAB_FAIL` (a stated failure) rather than on `U_HABIT_ANY`.
9. **`U_LEAVE_INTENT` excludes `SW_PAPER`.** In this corpus `SW_PAPER` is almost always inbound ("No more notebook!"), so it is counted as arrival in §0.7 and not as departure. The union definition in `n6-themes.py` records this.
10. **Quotes are verbatim.** Every quoted fragment was machine-checked to exist in that review's `title + "\n" + body` after NFKC and curly-quote normalisation. Ellipses mark omitted text; nothing is paraphrased inside quotation marks.
11. **No deduplication was applied.** All 7,069 records are counted, including the 17 that share normalised text with another (§9.H).

## 9.B Taxonomy — all 170 codes

Every code is hand-assigned. `n` is the number of reviews carrying it; `%` uses the 7,069 denominator; mean is the mean star rating of reviews carrying it.

## 9.C Validation, and what it caught

**Per-line validation at write time** (`n6-check-cls.py`, run after every 100-review batch, 71 times): index in range and unique; review ID matches the index; every code defined; no duplicate codes on a line; and **every quoted fragment present verbatim in that review**. Final state: **71 files, 7,069 lines, 0 errors.**

**Built-map validation** (`n6-validate.py`), six checks, all passing:

```
corpus            : 7069 reviews, 7069 unique ids
themes            : 166 codes, 18423 assignments
unassigned        : 0
mean codes/review : 2.61
ERRORS            : 0
```

The six checks are: (1) every theme ID exists in `reviews.jsonl`; (2) no intra-theme duplicate IDs; (3) no review assigned to zero themes; (4) `PER_REVIEW` covers every index exactly once with matching IDs; (5) every code defined and no duplicate codes per review; (6) `THEMES` counts reconcile exactly with `PER_REVIEW` counts.

**Four defined codes were never used** — `HAB_SWITCH_IN`, `HAB_SWITCH_OUT`, `NEG_SEARCH_BUG`, `PR_SEARCH` — because no review fitted them; a reviewer who left over routines was coded `HAB_FAIL` + `SW_TO_3P` rather than `HAB_SWITCH_OUT`, and search does not exist on iOS so cannot be praised or broken. They are listed in §9.B with n = 0 and are absent from §9.J.

**What the built-map and aggregation stage caught, and which is disclosed rather than hidden:**

| Class | Finding | Handling |
|---|---:|---|
| Union definition copied from a previous app | `U_LEAVE_INTENT` originally included `SW_PAPER`, which here is inbound (mean 4.41★) | Redefined to `SW_TO_3P`, `SW_TO_APPLE`, `SW_CONSIDER`, `HAB_SWITCH_OUT` before any number was written; disclosed in §9.A.9 |
| Coder boundary drift | `PR_CALVIEW` → `PR_GOOGLEINT` from 2024Q2; individual codes show a spurious 8.2% → 0.6% collapse and 4.3% → 14.7% rise; the union is flat (6.9–17.0% per quarter, no trend) | Neither code used alone for any time claim; union used in §7; disclosed in warning 5, §1.4, §7.1 |
| Possible coder-tolerance drift | `NOISE` 0.00% (E1) → 2.38% (E5); `CONTRA_RATING` 5.15% → 0.69% | `NOISE` carries no weight; the `CONTRA_RATING` decline is reported as a plausible real change (five-stars-for-potential faded) with the drift caveat attached (§4.7) |
| Pattern too loose in mechanical tests | `keep\b` matched "keep track" (306 hits); `assistant` matched generic use; `inbox` matched "inbox" generically | All three tightened and re-run; the table in §9.F shows the tightened results and says so |

**Report-level validation** (`n6-verify-ids.py`), run after writing: every review ID cited anywhere in this document exists in `reviews.jsonl`, and every `(#index, date, storefront, stars)` shown beside an ID matches the record. Result at §9.M.

**Known residual risk.** Single-coder judgement on adjacent codes, with no inter-rater statistic available. Mitigated by (a) the verbatim-quote anchor, (b) union-level reporting of every headline, (c) the sensitivity re-runs in §9.D, (d) the disclosed drift above.

**What changes band:** `NEG_NO_TIME` and `NEG_NO_RECUR` fall from Meaningful to Weak without E1 — they are launch-era complaints, exactly as §7.1 says. `NEG_NO_WIDGET` falls from High-priority to Very strong. `NEG_REMINDERS_MIGRATION` falls from Meaningful to Emerging without the 2023 window. `MON_WOULD_PAY` drops to Ignore-by-default without the migration window (6 reviews).

**What does not change:** every habit finding (`U_HABIT_TRACK_GAP` moves by 0.25 percentage points across all four cuts), every sharing finding, every money finding, every free-value finding, `NEG_CALSYNC`, and the direction of every praise code. **The central findings of this report are insensitive to both distortions.**

## 9.G Price points named by reviewers

The mechanical "price named" test returns 23 hits, of which 16 are phrases like "over a year" or "once a month". **Seven name a monetary amount**, plus one found by hand:

| Review | Amount | Context |
|---|---|---|
| `2467425833` (#37, 2018-04-25, it, 1★) | ~€7 | believes they paid for a free app — a mis-purchase of a third-party client |
| `2471776315` (#86, 2018-04-26, us, 5★) | $5 then $6/month | what they paid a competitor before switching *to* Tasks |
| `2475405006` (#119, 2018-04-27, ru, 1★) | 29 ₽ | a transaction after installing "for free" — mis-attributed |
| `2486803656` (#168, 2018-04-30, ru, 5★) | ~$15 | gTasks Pro, declined because the official app is free |
| `7874661381` (#3548, 2021-10-03, ru, 3★) | $12 | a "PRO" upgrade of a third-party client, bought in confusion |
| `9279639678` (#4399, 2022-11-11, us, 2★) | $6/year | a third-party client's subscription, resented |
| `9998367775` (#4740, 2023-06-04, au, 3★) | **$1–2 AUD/month, optional** | **the only offer to pay Google** |
| `11868525920` (#5752, 2024-10-24, jp, 5★) | ¥1,500 | a paid PC client, "satisfied" |

**One offer to pay Google in 7,069 reviews, at $1–2 AUD/month with "optional" attached; every other amount is money paid to someone other than Google, for a client of Google's data or for a competitor.** That is not a pricing study, and §8.7 says so.

## 9.H Burst, solicitation and authenticity checks

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Reviews flagged `is_edited` | 4 of 7,069 (0.06%) |
| Authors appearing more than once | 8 authors, twice each |
| Reviews sharing normalised text with another | **17 (0.24%)** across 6 distinct texts |
| Longest repeated text | **19 characters** — "great app great app" (2×) |
| Repeated texts longer than 60 characters | **0** |
| Referral / promo / giveaway language | **0** |
| Reviews with helpful votes | 931 (13.17%); most-voted review has 93 votes |

**No evidence of astroturfing, review farms, incentivised reviews or copy-paste campaigns.** The 17 duplicates are one- and two-word approval phrases.

**Solicited reviews** (`SOLICIT` = 7, 0.10%, mean 1.71★) exist but are below the ignore-by-default threshold (§3.9).

**Burst behaviour** is real and explained: launch month (175 reviews, 2018-04, mean 2.93★); the iOS 13 edit lock (2019-09: 131 reviews, 38.9% `NEG_EDIT_BROKEN`); the widget-demand peak (2021-01: 101 reviews, 24.8% `NEG_NO_WIDGET`); the April 2022 sort change; the 2023 Reminders migration (May–August); the Keep migration (2025-11 → 2026-02); the 2026 redesign (August–September). None is an authenticity problem; each is a product event and is dated in Part 7.

## 9.I Developer responses

**The schema contains no developer-response field**, so none could be analysed. `NEG_SUPPORT` = 35 (0.50%, 2.11★) records reviewers describing the absence of any feedback channel — `11261083531` (#5434, 2024-05-12, us, 3★) "I didn't know any other way to get this to the developers"; `7517187240` (#3351, 2021-06-28, us, 1★) "Hundreds of similar issues from 2019 and Google has yet to fix the issue". `PR_SUPPORT` = 10 (0.14%, 4.90★) are the reverse — mostly the September 2019 edit fix and three reviewers whose suggestion later shipped (`7851878699` #3534, 2021-09-27, cr, 5★ — "había recomendado hacer algunas mejoras y las hicieron perfecto" *[I had recommended some improvements and they did them perfectly]*).

## 9.M Post-write verification

Run after the narrative was complete, before Part 10 was appended (`Temp/n6-verify-ids.py`):

```
unique review IDs cited in the narrative (Parts 0–9, excluding the §9.J map) : 174
full citations checked (ID + #idx + date + store + stars)              : 165
IDs not present in reviews.jsonl                                        : 0
metadata mismatches                                                     : 0
(run over the whole document including §9.J: unique IDs 7069, not in corpus 0, mismatches 0)
```

Every review ID printed anywhere in this document exists in `reviews.jsonl`, and every index, date, storefront and star rating shown beside an ID matches that record exactly.

**How the IDs were kept honest:** no review ID in this report was written from memory. Every citation was copied from the evidence dump generated by `n6-ev.py` (which prints `review_id`, `#index`, date, storefront and stars straight from `reviews.jsonl` and the hand-coded quote fragments), and the finished text was then re-verified against the corpus by `n6-verify-ids.py`. **What this check caught during writing, and which is disclosed rather than hidden:** the first assembled draft contained **one** review ID with a single transposed leading digit (12232461252 written for 14232461252, #6917 — shown here without code formatting so the verifier does not read it as a citation), which the verifier flagged as not in the corpus; it was corrected from the working index before the report was finalised. No other ID or metadata mismatch was found.

**Also verified:** the theme→ID map reconciles exactly with the per-review index (§9.C check 6); the storefront table in §6.2 is generated directly from `reviews.jsonl` and `Tools/native_ratings.json` rather than transcribed; and the corpus totals in §1.3 are reproduced from `manifest.json` and `_state.json` with zero mismatches.
